points.name: 〜を通[とお]して / を通[つう]じて — through / via / throughout
points.shortDescription: Expresses that something is done through a medium/person, or throughout a period.
points.formation: Noun + を通[とお]して / を通[つう]じて + action or state
points.explanation:
を通[とお]して and を通[つう]じて (from 通[とお]す/通[つう]じる — to pass through, to connect through) both mean 'through,' 'via,' or 'throughout,' and in practice they are largely interchangeable. The distinctions that exist are subtle: を通[つう]じて sounds slightly more formal and is the preferred choice for set expressions about communication channels and institutional routes — 担当者[たんとうしゃ]を通[つう]じて (through the person in charge), 正式[せいしき]なルートを通[つう]じて (through official channels).

を通[とお]して is slightly more common for personal experiences and the sense of passing through something: この経験[けいけん]を通[とお]して多[おお]くを学[まな]んだ ('Through this experience I learned a lot'). For the 'throughout a period' use, both work equally well: 一年[いちねん]を通[とお]して/を通[つう]じて (throughout the year). In formal writing and business contexts, you can use either — native speakers mix them freely and the meaning is never unclear. When in doubt, を通[つう]じて adds a touch of formality.
rules: Noun + を通[とお]して / を通[つう]じて + action = through [medium] / via [medium]
Time noun + を通[とお]して / を通[つう]じて = throughout [period] (the whole time)
を通[つう]じて = slightly more formal; preferred for institutional channels and set expressions
を通[とお]して = slightly more common for personal experience or physical passage
Both appear in: business communication, academic writing, formal contexts

examples.japanese: SNSを通[つう]じて、多[おお]くの人[ひと]に情報[じょうほう]を発信[はっしん]することができます。

examples.japanese: この経験[けいけん]を通[とお]して、多[おお]くのことを学[まな]びました。
examples.romaji: Kono keiken wo tooshite, ooku no koto wo manabimashita.
examples.english: Through this experience, I learned many things.

examples.japanese: 一年[いちねん]を通[つう]じて、この地域[ちいき]は温暖[おんだん]な気候[きこう]です。
examples.romaji: Ichinen wo tsuujite, kono chiiki wa ondan na kikou desu.
examples.english: Throughout the year, this region has a warm climate.

examples.japanese: 友人[ゆうじん]の紹介[しょうかい]を通[とお]して、新[あたら]しい仕事[しごと]を見[み]つけることができました。
examples.romaji: Yuujin no shoukai wo tooshite, atarashii shigoto wo mitsukeru koto ga dekimashita.
examples.english: Through a friend's introduction, I was able to find new work.

points.flashcardAnswer: Expresses that something is done through a medium/person, or throughout a period.

practice.prompt: What does 〜を通[とお]して / 〜を通[つう]じて mean?
choices: without X
through / via / throughout — can mean through a medium/channel, or throughout a period
despite X
limited to X
practice.explanation: 〜を通[とお]して / 〜を通[つう]じて = through / via / throughout. 友人[ゆうじん]を通[とお]して知[し]り合[あ]った = met through a friend. 一年[いちねん]を通[とお]して温暖[おんだん]だ = warm throughout the year. Two main uses: (1) via/through a channel; (2) throughout a period.

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'He became famous through social media'?
choices: SNSを通[とお]して、彼[かれ]は有名[ゆうめい]になった。
SNSによって、彼[かれ]は有名[ゆうめい]になった。
SNSを使[つか]って、彼[かれ]は有名[ゆうめい]になった。
SNSのおかげで、彼[かれ]は有名[ゆうめい]になった。
practice.explanation: Noun + を通[とお]して: SNS + を通[とお]して = through social media (as a channel). 有名[ゆうめい]になった = became famous. を通[とお]して marks the medium through which the fame was achieved.

practice.prompt: Which means 'This region is warm throughout the year'?
choices: この地域[ちいき]は一年[いちねん]を通[とお]して温暖[おんだん]だ。
この地域[ちいき]は一年[いちねん]によって温暖[おんだん]だ。
この地域[ちいき]は一年[いちねん]を使[つか]って温暖[おんだん]だ。
この地域[ちいき]は一年[いちねん]のおかげで温暖[おんだん]だ。
practice.explanation: Noun (period) + を通[とお]して: 一年[いちねん] + を通[とお]して = throughout the year. 温暖[おんだん]だ = warm. を通[とお]して marks the entire span of the period throughout which the condition holds.

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'She learned Japanese through watching dramas'?
choices: ドラマを通[とお]して、彼女[かのじょ]は日本語[にほんご]を覚[おぼ]えた。
ドラマによって、彼女[かのじょ]は日本語[にほんご]を覚[おぼ]えた。
ドラマを使[つか]って、彼女[かのじょ]は日本語[にほんご]を覚[おぼ]えた。
ドラマのおかげで、彼女[かのじょ]は日本語[にほんご]を覚[おぼ]えた。
practice.explanation: Noun + を通[とお]して: ドラマ + を通[とお]して = through dramas (as a medium). 日本語[にほんご]を覚[おぼ]えた = learned Japanese. を通[とお]して marks dramas as the channel/medium for language learning.

practice.prompt: を通[とお]して vs. を通[つう]じて — what's the difference?
choices: They are identical
Largely interchangeable; を通[つう]じて is slightly more formal and common in official contexts; both mean 'through / via / throughout'
を通[つう]じて is only for time periods
を通[とお]して is only for physical channels — and this holds in every register, formal or casual.
practice.explanation: を通[とお]して and を通[つう]じて are largely interchangeable. を通[つう]じて is slightly more formal (common in official documents, news). 外務省[がいむしょう]を通[つう]じて = through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (formal). Both can express channel and time-throughout.

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'They communicated through an interpreter'?

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'She experienced various cultures through travel'?

points.name: 〜を抜[ぬ]きにして (wo nuki ni shite) — setting aside / without / leaving out
points.shortDescription: Sets aside or excludes something from consideration — 'without [X], we/it cannot...'.
points.formation: Noun + を抜[ぬ]きにして(は) + negative or assertion (often can't proceed without it)
points.explanation:
を抜[ぬ]きにして (from 抜[ぬ]く — to extract, to pull out) means 'setting aside,' 'leaving out,' or 'without' — and it does this in two related ways. First, deliberate exclusion: 冗談[じょうだん]を抜[ぬ]きにして、真剣[しんけん]に話[はな]しましょう — 'Setting jokes aside, let's talk seriously' — we're explicitly putting something to one side to clear the air.

Second, and more powerfully, を抜[ぬ]きにしては + negative highlights indispensability: 彼女[かのじょ]を抜[ぬ]きにしては、このチームは成[な]り立[た]ちません — 'Without her, this team cannot function.' Remove her hypothetically, and everything collapses — which is the highest form of praise. The は after を抜[ぬ]きにしては adds the conditional 'if we were to exclude X' edge. This pattern elegantly does double duty: it can exclude something from consideration, and — by the indispensability framing — it can honor something as absolutely irreplaceable. Compare なしには (without, similar meaning) — を抜[ぬ]きにしては is more emphatic and formal in register.
rules: Noun + を抜[ぬ]きにして = setting aside [noun] / without [noun] (excluding from consideration)
〜を抜[ぬ]きにしては + negative = without [noun], [negative] (highlights indispensability)
Used both to exclude something and to emphasize something is indispensable
Related: 〜なしには (without) — similar but を抜[ぬ]きにしては more emphatic
Common: 冗談[じょうだん]を抜[ぬ]きにして (setting jokes aside), お世辞[せじ]を抜[ぬ]きにして (setting flattery aside)

examples.japanese: 彼女[かのじょ]を抜[ぬ]きにしては、このチームは成[な]り立[た]ちません。
examples.romaji: Kanojo wo nuki ni shite wa, kono chiimu wa naritachimasen.
examples.english: Without her, this team cannot function.

examples.japanese: 冗談[じょうだん]を抜[ぬ]きにして、真剣[しんけん]に考[かんが]えてほしいのです。
examples.romaji: Joudan wo nuki ni shite, shinken ni kangaete hoshii no desu.
examples.english: Setting jokes aside, I want you to think about this seriously.

examples.japanese: あなたの協力[きょうりょく]を抜[ぬ]きにしては、このプロジェクトを完成[かんせい]させることはできません。
examples.romaji: Anata no kyouryoku wo nuki ni shite wa, kono purojekuto wo kansei saseru koto wa dekimasen.
examples.english: Without your cooperation, we cannot complete this project.

examples.japanese: お世辞[せじ]を抜[ぬ]きにして言[い]えば、今回[こんかい]の発表[はっぴょう]はとてもよかったです。
examples.romaji: Oseji wo nuki ni shite ieba, konkai no happyou wa totemo yokatta desu.
examples.english: Setting flattery aside and speaking honestly, the presentation this time was very good.

points.flashcardAnswer: Sets aside or excludes something from consideration — 'without [X], we/it cannot...'.

practice.prompt: What does 〜を抜[ぬ]きにして mean?
choices: including X
setting aside / without / leaving out X — often implies that without X, something cannot function or proceed properly
thanks to X
contrary to X
practice.explanation: 〜を抜[ぬ]きにして = setting aside / without X. 冗談[じょうだん]を抜[ぬ]きにして話[はな]しましょう = let's talk without joking. 彼[かれ]を抜[ぬ]きにしてはチームが成[な]り立[た]たない = without him, the team can't function. Often paired with は for emphasis.

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'Let's think about this leaving aside money matters'?
choices: お金[かね]のことを抜[ぬ]きにして考[かんが]えましょう。
お金[かね]のことなしに考[かんが]えましょう。
お金[かね]のことを除[のぞ]いて考[かんが]えましょう。
お金[かね]のことを無視[むし]して考[かんが]えましょう。
practice.explanation: Noun + を抜[ぬ]きにして: お金[かね]のこと + を抜[ぬ]きにして = setting aside money matters. 考[かんが]えましょう = let's think. を抜[ぬ]きにして removes X from the equation so the main point can be addressed.

practice.prompt: Which means 'Without her, this project would not have succeeded'?
choices: 彼女[かのじょ]を抜[ぬ]きにしては、このプロジェクトは成功[せいこう]しなかっただろう。

practice.prompt: 〜を抜[ぬ]きにしては vs. 〜を抜[ぬ]きにして — what's the difference in nuance?

を抜[ぬ]きにしては is incorrect Japanese, with no exceptions in modern standard Japanese — textbooks treat this as an absolute rule.

points.name: 〜をはじめとして (wo hajime to shite) — starting with / including / such as
points.shortDescription: Names a primary example as the representative of a broader group.
points.formation: Noun (primary example) + をはじめとして / をはじめとする + broader group
points.explanation:
をはじめとして (from 始[はじ]める — to start with) is the grammar of the prime example: it introduces the most prominent or representative member of a group, then extends to the broader category. 社長[しゃちょう]をはじめとして、全社[ぜんしゃ]員[いん]が賛同[さんどう]した — 'Starting with the company president, all employees agreed' — the president is the most prominent representative, and the agreement extends outward to everyone.

The structure is clearly hierarchical: the most important or representative element comes before をはじめとして; the broader group or description of it follows after. The attributive form をはじめとする modifies nouns directly: 東京[とうきょう]をはじめとする大都市[だいとし] ('major cities, with Tokyo as the prime example').

This is formal and standard in announcements, reports, and official writing where you want to lead with the flagship example before gesturing to the rest. More specific and formal than たとえば (for example) or など (etc.).
rules: Primary Noun + をはじめとして = starting with / including (names rep. example, extends to group)
Attributive: をはじめとする + Noun = [noun] including / led by [primary example]
The noun before をはじめとして is the most important/representative element
More formal and specific than たとえば (for example) or など (etc.)
Common in formal announcements, academic writing, and business documents

examples.japanese: 社長[しゃちょう]をはじめとして、全社[ぜんしゃ]員[いん]が新[あたら]しい方針[ほうしん]に賛同[さんどう]しました。
examples.romaji: Shachou wo hajime to shite, zen shain ga atarashii houshin ni sandou shimashita.
examples.english: Starting with the company president, all employees agreed with the new policy.

examples.japanese: 英語[えいご]をはじめとする外国語教育[がいこくごきょういく]が、学校[がっこう]で重視[じゅうし]されています。
examples.romaji: Eigo wo hajime to suru gaikokugo kyouiku ga, gakkou de juushi sarete imasu.
examples.english: Foreign language education, including English, is being emphasized in schools.

examples.japanese: 東京[とうきょう]をはじめとして、大阪[おおさか]や名古屋[なごや]でも展示会[てんじかい]が開催[かいさい]される予定[よてい]です。
examples.romaji: Tokyo wo hajime to shite, Osaka ya Nagoya demo tenjikai ga kaisai sareru yotei desu.
examples.english: Starting in Tokyo, an exhibition is also planned to be held in Osaka and Nagoya.

examples.japanese: 山田[やまだ]さんをはじめとするベテラン社員[しゃいん]の経験[けいけん]が、会社[かいしゃ]を支[ささ]えています。
examples.romaji: Yamada-san wo hajime to suru beteran shain no keiken ga, kaisha wo sasaete imasu.
examples.english: The experience of veteran employees including Yamada-san is supporting the company.

points.flashcardAnswer: Names a primary example as the representative of a broader group.

practice.prompt: What does 〜をはじめとして mean?
choices: only X / limited to X
starting with X / including X / X and others like X — takes X as the prime or most representative example of a broader group
because of X
without X
practice.explanation: 〜をはじめとして = starting with X / including X. 東京[とうきょう]をはじめとして、多[おお]くの都市[とし]でイベントが開催[かいさい]された = starting with Tokyo, events were held in many cities. X (the prime example) + をはじめとして + the broader category.

practice.prompt: をはじめとして vs. をはじめとする — what's the difference?
choices: They are completely different
をはじめとして: adverbial (modifies the main clause); をはじめとする: attributive (modifies a noun). Meaning is the same: 'starting with X'
をはじめとする is more casual
をはじめとして can only be used with people — this is true in both spoken and written Japanese.
practice.explanation: をはじめとして (adverbial): 東京[とうきょう]をはじめとして、多[おお]くの都市[とし]で = starting with Tokyo, in many cities . をはじめとする (attributive): 東京[とうきょう]をはじめとする多[おお]くの都市[とし] = many cities starting with Tokyo . Both mean 'starting with / including X.'

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'Starting with rice, Japan produces various agricultural products'?

practice.prompt: をはじめとして marks X as what in relation to the group that follows?
choices: The least representative member, and the rule applies to every sentence type.
The MOST REPRESENTATIVE or most prominent example — X is the prime case, and the broader group follows
The most surprising member
The exception to the group
practice.explanation: X + をはじめとして: X is the most prominent or representative member of a group. 東京[とうきょう]をはじめとする都市[とし] = cities, with Tokyo as the most prominent (prime) example. X is always the top/best-known member, and をはじめとして introduces it as the leading example before expanding to the broader category.

practice.prompt: をはじめとして can be shortened to をはじめ. Which example shows this correct usage?

practice.prompt: をはじめとして vs. など — which is more FORMAL and emphasizes X as the LEADING example?
choices: They are identical
をはじめとして is more formal and explicitly marks X as the MOST PROMINENT example; など is casual ('X and so on' — doesn't emphasize rank)
など is more formal
をはじめとして is more casual, with no exceptions in modern standard Japanese — textbooks treat this as an absolute rule.
practice.explanation: をはじめとして: more formal, X is the prime/most prominent: 東京[とうきょう]をはじめとして多[おお]くの都市[とし]で (Tokyo, as the prime example, and many other cities). など: casual, X is just one of many: 東京[とうきょう]などの都市[とし]で (cities like Tokyo). をはじめとして highlights X's prominence; など just lists loosely.
